1:
Henry begins with the surprise of it. One would wonder that Jerusalem, the holy city where God was known, should bear so black a character, and that a place enjoying such means of grace should grow so corrupt; but so it is, to show that the law made nothing perfect. The holy God hates sin in those nearest to him, Henry says, and in them hates it most, so that a sinful state is and will be a woeful state. He takes the charge in three parts. She shames herself, being filthy and polluted, or as others read it made infamous, or as the margin has it the gluttonous city, always cramming and making provision for the flesh. She wrongs her own inhabitants, since no place ever had statutes so righteous and none saw more unrighteousness in administering them. And she walks contrary to her God at every point: he gave his law and spoke by his prophets, and she obeyed not; he put her under the discipline of word and rod, and she received neither instruction nor correction; he encouraged her to depend on his promise, and her confidence went into alliances with the nations; he gave her ordinances of communion, and she would not meet him where he had promised to meet her, but stood at a distance and said to the Almighty, Depart.

Calvin fastens on the same paradox. Jerusalem might seem superior because God had not chosen it in vain as the place of his worship, but the prophet shows how empty that boasting was. He hears in the word polluted an allusion to the washings of the law, which could not themselves take away filth but were meant to teach a holy manner of worship; since they washed often and kept the rites of outward sanctity while missing their design, the prophet derides their hypocrisy and calls them defiled in their whole life though in appearance the purest of all. Gill lists the filth as murders and adulteries and oppression and rapine, and makes the same point about appearances: they were pure in their own eyes though not washed from their filthiness, cleaning the outside of the cup while within they were full of impurity.

Which Jerusalem is meant divides them. Gill argues that it is not the city before the captivity but the city of the second temple, and of the times at the coming of Christ, since the intimations of the conversion of the Gentiles and of a state in which the people shall see evil no more can suit no other times than those of the Gospel. Clarke reads the chapter on the same principle, laying out its plan as reproof, then encouragement to look for mercy once chastised, then hymns of joy, and last large promises belonging to the days of the Messiah; he defends so extensive a view by an apostle's assurance that every prophetical book contains predictions relating to the Gospel.

On the four refusals of the second verse the voices agree. Gill takes the voice for that of the prophets and carries the charge forward, that they hearkened neither to the forerunner who gave notice of Christ's coming, nor to Christ himself, nor to the apostles whose doctrine they contradicted. Wesley makes the voice God's own, crying aloud by mercies and judgments, and Clarke adds conscience to God and the prophets. Clarke glosses each clause: she did not profit by chastisement but was ill-tempered under affliction; she did not consider God the fountain from which all help should come, but sought support from herself; she did not worship or walk in his ways or make supplication. Ellicott would render the first clause as hearkened not to the voice, and sharpens the two negatives into contrasts: she trusted not in the Lord but in her own wealth, and drew near not to her God but to Baal and Moloch.
3:
Gill notes that the comparison is implied rather than stated, the note of similitude being wanting in the Hebrew and supplied by the old versions, so that the princes are as roaring lions. He takes them for civil magistrates rather than princes of the blood, and carries the charge into the Gospel history, where such men gaped on the Lord of glory like ravening lions and afterwards breathed out threatenings against his disciples. Clarke has them tearing all to pieces without a shadow of law beyond their own despotic power, and explains the second figure by the hours: the judges, a little afraid of the lion-like princes, do their unjust dealing between evening and morning and take the day for rest, turning day into night by their revelling. Wesley gives the wolves their hunger, insatiable and cruel.

The last clause is read three ways. Wesley takes it as the received version has it, that they leave nothing but the bones to be eaten on the morrow. Clarke divides the meal in time, the flesh devoured at night and the bones gnawed afterwards. Ellicott says the received sense is exactly wrong: the clause should read on the morrow, and means they are so greedy they devour the prey at once and leave nothing for the next day. Calvin is interested not in the beasts but in the order of society they describe. He had called the city rapacious, and now proves it, since even where no justice is regarded among the people some shame usually remains in the judges to keep them within limits; but when robbery is practised in the court of justice, what is to be said of such a city? He notes that the prophets, meaning to condemn all from the least to the greatest, addressed themselves particularly to the judges.

Who these prophets were is disputed. Gill takes them for the false prophets and identifies them with the interpreters of the law met with in the Gospels, calling them light in knowledge, empty-headed and unstable and compliant with the humours of the people; he reports another rendering drawn from the Arabic, that the word means proud, since men of superficial knowledge boasted of much and carried themselves insolently. Ellicott renders the pair as braggarts and men of treachery. Calvin prefers empty or men of nought, taking the word for the rash and those void of judgment and moderation, as though the prophet had said they were stupid and blind; and he observes that fraudulence is the quality most inconsistent with the prophetic office, and that in calling such men prophets at all he is making a concession. Clarke says such men have no deep conviction of the awful nature of their office and no concern for the souls of the people, and betray them for worldly honour and profit.

On doing violence to the law the voices agree closely. Wesley calls it wresting the law by perverse interpretation; Clarke says they forced wrong constructions on it to excuse themselves and lull the people into spiritual slumber, wresting the Scriptures being an ancient practice. Calvin draws a different lesson from the whole indictment. There was then no Church of God except at Jerusalem, and yet judges and prophets and priests are declared apostate together, so that one may ask what comfort was left to the faithful; the answer is that the fear of God had not failed in his elect, who contended with an invincible heart. He presses the point. Zephaniah stood almost alone, taught alongside Jeremiah when hardly two or three discharged the office faithfully, and the false prophets were bolder for their numbers; yet he did not cease to cry against them, and no union formed by men can lessen the authority of God. Let the few, Calvin says, not be disheartened when they see the worship of God perverted, but resist thousands if need be.
5:
The sentence cuts both ways, and the voices take it in opposite directions. Gill hears an aggravation of the guilt just described: the Lord was in the midst of the very city where those princes and judges and prophets and priests were, seeing and observing all their evil actions, and yet they were neither deterred by the presence of one who loves righteousness and hates iniquity nor allured by his example. He then applies the title. This character of the just Lord agrees with Christ, who is perfectly righteous in both his natures and in the execution of his offices and is the author of righteousness to his people, and Gill would understand the clause of his personal presence in that city and in the temple, where he taught his doctrine and wrought his miracles. Wesley reduces the whole verse to a series of glosses: in the midst means observing all; he will not do iniquity means he will judge them righteously; every morning means that daily he discovers his displeasure against the wicked; he faileth not means he lets no season slip to convince them by public and visible punishments; and the last clause means that the wicked go on without shame and without fear. Clarke says the same of the first clause, that he sees and marks down and will punish, and reports a paraphrase of the second from another writer, that not a day passes but we see instances of God's goodness to righteous men and of his vengeance on the wicked.

Calvin reads the clause as a quotation turned back on the men who used it. The Jews had this boast always on their lips, that they were still the holy people of God and that he dwelt in the midst of them, since he was worshipped in a temple built not at men's will but by his command, and the word that appointed it came from heaven and called that place his rest for ever. The prophet concedes exactly what they claim, but to the opposite purpose, so that they might understand his hand was near to punish their sins. Granted, Calvin has him say, he does dwell in this city; he commanded a temple to be built for him here and ordered a holy altar; but then consider what kind of God it is who dwells here. When he purposed to dwell among you he did not deny himself or cease to be what he is, and there is no reason to imagine that for the sake of those he bound himself to he meant to lay aside his own justice, or to let himself be polluted by the defilements of men. He will not approve your evil deeds; and though he may connive at them for a time, he will not bear with them for ever, so there is no ground for flattering yourselves that God approves what you do.

What the clause about not doing iniquity means Calvin settles by rejecting one reading and reporting another. Some apply it to the people, as though the sense were that they ought not to have done iniquity; that Calvin calls a strained exposition and altogether foreign to the context. Most interpreters, he says, take it of God himself, that he is just and will do no wrong, since he had sufficient reason for executing vengeance on so wicked a people; on that view the prophet is anticipating a murmur, and forestalling the complaint that the Lord was cruel or too rigid, so that however grievous the punishment inflicted the Jews could not arraign him as unjust.
6:
Which nations were cut off the voices answer from different quarters. Gill points back through the preceding chapters to the Philistines and Moabites and Ethiopians and Assyrians, all destroyed before the coming of Christ in the flesh, and says the Jews should have taken warning from them. Wesley reaches further back and further forward at once, naming the Canaanites of old, then the ten tribes, and later the Assyrians. Ellicott divides them the same way, into those destroyed by the agency of Israel on entering the land and those cut off by the Assyrians and the other great powers God used as instruments, and Clarke reports a shorter list of Syria and Israel from another writer. Calvin cares less which they were than how many. God warned the Jews not by one example but by many, having manifested himself a judge on every side by punishing one nation after another; a people who could not be instructed by the calamities of others were past hope. Had they been in a sane mind, their own quiet while God spared them should have made them ask what they deserved, on the principle that what is done in the green tree will at length be done in the dry. Calvin sharpens the argument by comparison: an ordinary punishment is easily disregarded, but when God showed by such remarkable proofs that he was displeased with the nations, who beside the Jews were ignorant and comparatively innocent, only men wholly irreclaimable could have taken no warning. He gives the verse in a plainer rendering, that the towers became desolate, the streets empty without a passenger, the cities deserted without a man and without an inhabitant, and notes that one line reads literally that their cities were hunted, so that none was left behind.

The next verse is read either as a divine soliloquy or as an unanswered wish. Gill takes it after the manner of men, as though God reasoned within himself that the people would surely notice his judgments on other nations and fear to offend, which humanly speaking might reasonably have been expected. Wesley says the same in a line, I thought, speaking after the manner of men. Calvin allows the figure but guards it: God assumes the character of a man here as he often does elsewhere, not because he waits on a future he is doubtful of, since all things are before his eyes. Ellicott renders the clause quite differently, as a question or wish rather than an expectation, wouldest thou only fear me, wouldest thou receive correction, and then her dwelling-place should not be destroyed according to all that God had appointed for them; and he takes the appointment to mean what was appointed in the way of punishment. The lament over the city in the Gospels, he adds, naturally suggests itself here. Keil and Delitzsch renders it similarly as an entreaty, only do thou fear me, do thou accept correction, so will their dwelling not be cut off, and reads these two verses as the summing up of everything said from the opening of the chapter, closing the call to repentance with the announcement of judgment.

On the last clause the voices converge. Keil and Delitzsch has them most zealously destroying all their doings; Ellicott, that they only speeded their infamous doings. Clarke supplies the picture: after so many displays of sovereign power they did not return to God but practised every abomination, and were diligent to find out times and places for their iniquity, which he calls the worst state of man. Calvin has already given the reason for the whole passage, that a people so often warned and still unmoved were plainly blinded by their own wickedness, and that they hastened the very judgment God had meant these examples to stay.
8:
Who is told to wait is the sharpest disagreement in the chapter. Gill takes the word as addressed to the few who feared the Lord and received Christ's doctrine, encouraged to wait for him and expect that he would work deliverance when distress came on the unbelieving. Keil and Delitzsch argues the same from usage: the summons returns the prophecy to its starting point, and those addressed are the meek of the earth already called to seek the Lord; the nation as such cannot be meant, since the command would then have to be read ironically, and the verb is used only of waiting in a believing attitude. Henry finds the whole grace of the passage there. Everything in the preceding verses points toward a city abandoned as reprobate silver, and instead comes an invitation, so that we may wonder at a divine grace which takes occasion from man's badness to appear the more illustrious; since the law will make nothing perfect, the bringing in of a better hope shall, and those who lament the corruptions of the church may wait upon God until he send his Son to save his people from their sins and purify to himself a peculiar people of both Jews and Gentiles. There were such waiters, Henry adds, who looked for redemption in that very city, and what was long looked for came at last.

Calvin dissents, and knows he is dissenting. Some think the address is made to the faithful, that they might prepare to bear the cross; that view, he says, is foreign to the prophet's subject, and though it has gained the consent of almost all he does not doubt that this is a complaint rather than an invitation. God is done dealing in words with a people so irreclaimable, and the sense is that he stands present and fully prepared: he had tried to turn them and their hearts were hardened, he had set examples on every side among the heathen and effected nothing, and now he will contend with them no longer nor send them prophets again. Rising up to the prey Calvin refuses to render for ever, as some do, and takes instead for a threat of plunder, God forgetting the kindness that had only been a sport to them and coming as a wild beast comes, as lions rage and tear and devour, because he had hitherto spared them too paternally. Wesley reads the verse the same way: since they will not be amended, they are to attend his resolution, and the indignation falls upon the incorrigible.

The gathering of the nations is read by scale. Calvin says the nations and kingdoms are named so that the Jews might understand judgment could no longer be deferred, since judgment begins at the house of God and they were less excusable than unbelievers who went astray in darkness for want of the light. Henry hears the summons of the gospel preached to every creature, all nations called as it were to appear before the Redeemer setting up his kingdom, and the indignation poured on those who will not obey the summons; the distress of nations with perplexity belongs to that same moment. On the last clause the voices part again over its extent. Clarke confines it, glossing all the earth as all the land of Judah, and states the ground of the whole verse in a line, that we are to expect the fulfilment of all his promises and threatenings because he is God and changes not. Calvin extends it, so that no corner of the earth may escape that hand. Henry extends it too, and makes both Jews and Gentiles answerable for their enmity to the gospel. Wesley explains the fire itself, as a jealousy with which God is jealous for his own glory, and the devouring as a being consumed as though burnt up.
9:
Calvin explains why a promise follows the threat. Had the prophet said only that God meant to gather the nations and devour the whole earth, the faithful could have concluded nothing but that they would perish with the rest, so something had to be added to inspire hope. He notes the habit behind it: the prophet speaks at one time to the whole body of the people and at another to the few, as a man addressing a crowd reproves the multitude severely and then shapes his words to those with whom he has less fault to find. Here he collects the remnant by themselves and sets pardon before them.

Whose lip is purified divides them. Keil and Delitzsch reports a reading in which the pure lip is God's own, turned toward the nations through his holy servants, so that the promise is to have the nations preached to with friendly lips; he sets it out in order to reject it. Calvin rejects it in the same terms: it is evidently not the language God would use in addressing the nations but the language they would use in addressing him, and what is meant is a pure heart, the organ of speech being put for the heart, as the shoulder is afterwards put for the service rendered. Wesley agrees in a line: a pure way of worshipping God, issuing from a pure heart. Clarke goes further and makes the phrase mean the form of religious worship itself, since the people had been idolaters and God promises to restore his worship among them; he supports the sense from another passage where the same words mean a religious confession rather than a spoken tongue. Ellicott takes the figure as language proper, the discord of Babel giving place to unity when many gods yield to one. Gill takes the turning as reciprocal, God changing his speech toward the nations by sending them the Gospel after centuries in which he sent them no prophet, and their speech toward him being changed in turn.

The dispersed are claimed by both sides. Calvin knows that some refer the verse to the Gentiles and argues against them: the phrase daughter of the dispersion cannot be applied to the Ethiopians, the proper names some find here answer to no known nation, and the sense is that Jews would return out of the farthest region to offer sacrifice, coming in with the Gentiles so that both should agree in one faith. Wesley and Clarke read it the same way, of the praying remnant of the scattered people. Ellicott flatly reverses it: the dispersed are not Jewish exiles but the Gentile tribes of the dispersion, alienated from their Creator by ignorance and vice, so that the new Church draws adherents even from the southern limit of the known world; he compares the unwitting prophecy of the high priest that Christ should gather into one the scattered children of God. Gill hunts for the fulfilment rather than arguing the reference, and finds it either in the preaching carried into that country and the conversion of the eunuch, or, if the rivers are boundary rivers, in the neighbouring land promised elsewhere as speaking the language of Canaan.

On the offering Ellicott notes that the word is the bloodless oblation and here means homage rendered as to a sovereign, and reports a rendering in which men bring the suppliants rather than the suppliants bringing the gift, which he thinks wrong. Clarke reads it as their acknowledgment of the mercy that sent them the Messiah to turn every one from his iniquities. Calvin allows a further possibility from the root, that the word for suppliants may be passive and mean those reconciled to God, so that God is at length propitious to exiles cast away beyond those rivers; but he judges that too forced and keeps to suppliants coming from the utmost parts.
11:
Why the shame ends is disputed. Gill grounds it on pardon: the doings will not be continued in but repented of, and being forgiven and remembered no more they cannot be charged home; he adds that shame still arises from a true sense of sin, and the more when sin is seen in the glass of pardoning love, but that such men are not ashamed to appear before God and can stand in his sight with holy confidence. Calvin reports and refuses another reading, that the verse speaks not of the remission of sins but of the holy life that follows regeneration, so that nothing in the conduct would remain to blush for; that he calls strained and impossible to fit to the words, since the text names the doings wherein thou hast transgressed, which can only be referred to forgiveness. Clarke states it plainly, that the punishment shall cease because God pardons the sin.

What is taken away is described in three registers. Clarke names the wicked priests and scribes who would not come under Christ's yoke; Wesley calls them proud formalists; Ellicott turns to what they were proud of, since the adoption and the covenants and the temple service had all been used as a pretext for obduracy, so that we have Abraham for our father, and the temple of the Lord are these, were the answers returned to the preaching of repentance, and the reinstated nation is to be purged of that pride. Clarke and Wesley alike hear in the last clause a promise that they will boast no more in the temple. Calvin sets the whole against the grief of the survivors. It was bitter that hardly a tenth part should remain, and the ruin of their brethren affected the faithful deeply, as one apostle felt for his own nation when he saw it alienated from God; so the prophet offers a compensation, that by this small number God would at last be purely served.

The people left behind are drawn as the exact reverse of those removed. Gill lists what afflicted means for the Lord's people in every age, a body of sin, the temptations of Satan, the hidings of God's face, bodily infirmities, and the persecutions of men; and what poor means, mostly the poor of this world stripped of their goods for Christ's sake, but chiefly poor in spirit, broken-hearted and holding a mean opinion of themselves. Ellicott points to a play in the Hebrew, that the word for afflicted names a condition likely to make men meek, the near neighbour of that word, instead of haughty. Calvin makes the same connection an argument about method. Pride could not be torn out unless they were wholly cast down, for as long as they remained whole they were always proud; had they been willingly teachable there would have been no need of so severe a correction, and they had to be broken because they could not be bent. He would render the pair a people humbled and reduced, the first meaning one made low by distress rather than naturally lowly, the second one brought to poverty, so that they could not be corrected without being stripped of every material of their glorying.

Of the remnant Gill says they are the few reserved according to the election of grace, who on being convinced of sin forsake their former course; and he guards the promise from being read too absolutely, since it does not mean they will be without sin but that they will not live in it. Clarke does not analyse the promise but exclaims at it, that this will be a change indeed and will leave them wholly unlike what they now are, with iniquity and lying and deceit not to be found among them.
14:
Henry marks where the chapter has arrived: after promises of the taking away of sin come promises of the taking away of trouble, for when the cause is removed the effect will cease, and what makes a people holy will make them happy of course. He presses the terms of the summons, that the joy is to be inward and to be great, since those who love God with all their heart have occasion with all their heart to rejoice in him; and he ties it back to the verse before, that those who reform have cause to rejoice, whereas a people cannot rejoice for joy like others while it goes a whoring from its God. Calvin explains why the prophet speaks as though the thing were already done. The prophets encourage hope by stirring up gratitude, congratulating the faithful on blessings still remote as if they were in possession of what they had only prayed for; and he was not earnest here without reason, since it is hard to console the afflicted while God gives the flesh no evidence of hope, so that this heap of words was meant to fortify them for severe trials. Calvin weighs the four verbs closely: the first two call for the fullest expression of feeling, a loud cry and a shout like a trumpet, and the second pair name what the feeling is, joy and exultation, so that be glad and rejoice is too feeble for what stands there. Gill supplies the grounds of the song, the coming of Christ and redemption by him, the Gospel and its ordinances, and the numbers converted of both Jews and Gentiles; and Clarke says the verse promises not only restoration from captivity but conversion to God through Christ.

What the taken-away judgments were is read at different depths. Ellicott keeps to the plain connection, that God removes what he had earlier appointed concerning them in the way of punishment. Wesley says the same, that the judgments their sins had brought on them are abolished and ended. Henry itemises them, the noise of war silenced, the reproach of famine done away and the captivity brought back, and adds a distinction: though some grievances remain they will be afflictions only and not judgments, because the sin is pardoned. Gill goes furthest and makes the judgments inward as well as outward, so that not only exile and poverty and reproach among the nations are removed but hardness of heart and blindness of mind and unbelief, when the power of divine grace brings them to a sense of sin.

The enemy is identified variously. Wesley names the Babylonian. Henry describes him as one who had thrust himself into the land and triumphed there, and prefers a rendering that has him swept out as dirt is swept out of a house to the dunghill, with the moral that when a people sweep out their sins with the besom of reformation God will sweep out their enemies. On the king in the midst Clarke reads a plain messianic promise, since they have had no king since the death of Zedekiah and will have none until the King Messiah reigns among them. Ellicott looks at the title rather than the date, noting that the recognition of the Lord himself as king is a prominent feature elsewhere in the portrait of the enlarged dispensation, where it is said among the heathen that the Lord is king and that the kingdom shall be his. Wesley reads the presence as a return, that he is come back to redeem and govern; and he attaches a condition to the last clause, that while their carriage is as becomes his presence with them they shall neither fear nor feel the like evils again.
16:
Who does the saying is left open. Calvin allows either the prophets or the common report of mankind, and thinks it makes no great difference which; either way Jerusalem would be so tranquil that the congratulation would be offered on every side. Gill runs through the same possibilities and settles on the Lord himself, following the old versions, ruling out only the enemies as speakers; and he divides the fear into outward enemies and inward spiritual ones, sin and Satan and death and hell, all vanquished by Christ. Clarke reads it as promising no more captivities nor national afflictions.

The slack hands are read as an image of what fear costs a man. Calvin says all vigour is so relaxed by fear that no member can do its office, and takes the hands for the whole body, since by the hands men perform their works; when fear prevails we are as lifeless and cannot raise a finger, but when hope animates us there is vigour through the whole body. He insists on the connection between a quiet state and busy hands: God does not free his people from trouble that they may grow torpid, but that they may attend the more to their duty. Clarke applies the clause first to the rebuilding of the temple after the return and then to diligence and zeal in the Christian Church.

On the seventeenth verse the voices take the words apart singly. Gill treats each as an antidote against fear: he is in the midst to support and defend, not merely by the essential presence which is everywhere or the providential presence which reaches all creatures, but by a gracious presence peculiar to his people; he is the Lord, eternal and immutable; he is their God, God in their nature; and he is mighty, able to save to the uttermost. Clarke works from the Hebrew to the same end, that the name is that of the self-existent Being in covenant with them, and that the word for mighty means the prevailing One, the all-conquering hero, the title given elsewhere to the child that is born. He glosses the saving as deliverance from the power and guilt and pollution of sin, and would render the rest in his love as a renewal of it. Ellicott renders the middle clause differently, that he will keep silence in his love and exult over thee with a shout of joy, and explains the pair as two expressions of a bridegroom's love, unutterable yearning and jubilant outburst alike, ascribed to God by a bold anthropomorphism.

Who is gathered in the last verse is disputed in detail. Gill offers two readings, either those kept from the place of worship by distance or infirmity or persecution, since to be denied the means of grace troubles gracious souls, or those sorrowing for the appointed time of deliverance which seems delayed. Wesley keeps to the first, those mourning their distance from the solemn worship of God. Clarke sets them in the captivity, mourning for their former assemblies and reproached by enemies who knew they could not keep their solemnities, as in the psalm sung by the rivers of Babylon. Ellicott takes the coming festival as figured by the Feast of Tabernacles, at which none shall be impeded because the oppressors will be overthrown, and renders the last clause as those on whom reproach lay as a burden. Calvin fixes on the word for time, which he says means not time simply but a determined season. The prophet holds the faithful in suspense so that they may keep to their watch tower and wait, for we run headlong when we hope for anything, and that haste is often our own delay; God will fulfil his promise not soon nor at the will of men but when the fit time comes, which is the time he has appointed and not the one we desire.
19:
The opening verb is weighed. Gill notes that it is simply I will do, the old versions supplying the object, one rendering it slay and another an entire destruction; Ellicott would render it I will deal with, and Calvin agrees that this is the literal sense, observing that more is implied than expressed. He also records that some amend the clause into conformity with the Greek, and calls that a very unsafe process. Clarke reports another rendering, that God will work with thee for thy sake at that time, and grants the original is obscure enough to bear it. Wesley states the effect, that God will break their power and dissolve their kingdom. Clarke supplies the reason: it shows much baseness of mind to afflict those already under the chastising hand of God, and he instances the Edomites and Moabites and Ammonites, who did exactly that and were severely punished for it.

Her that halteth is the weakest of the flock. Gill takes her for one weak in faith who cannot walk except haltingly, like a lame and maimed sheep; Wesley says one in trouble and ready to fall. Clarke points to a parallel promise in another prophet, refers the gathering of the driven out to the captivity, and suggests the figure may be the renewing of a covenant with a spouse divorced for unfaithfulness and now brought back. On the praise and fame he expects a total change of character, so that they shall become great and good and useful and be as eminent for excellence in the lands where they sojourned as they had been for the opposite.

Calvin uses the verse to press patience rather than describe the deliverance. God would overcome every obstacle once his purpose was to restore his people, and the prophet dwells on that so the exiles might hope for a thing the flesh could not conceive as possible. But the words at that time repeat what has been said, that they must wait as long as God pleases to exercise them under the cross; had the choice been theirs they would have stayed at their ease, since men naturally desire immunity from evil. Calvin therefore condemns again the extreme haste that takes hold of men under chastisement, and insists that however slowly God proceeds in delivering his own there is no reason to despair.

On the last verse Gill joins the two gatherings, so that when the Lord calls them effectually to himself he returns them to their own land, where they will be gathered into one body and appoint themselves one head. Clarke dates it first from the end of the seventy years of the captivity and makes that restoration a type of a later redemption from sin, adding that only then will they have a name and a praise among all the people of the earth. On the closing phrase he reports a variant, that some read before their eyes, meaning the eyes of all peoples. Calvin explains why the promise is repeated: nobody thought a people cast as it were into the grave would come out of it, still less be raised to such dignity. He makes a point of the plural, since the word is captivities, and blames interpreters who render it as one: the people had not merely been driven into exile but scattered through many countries, so that they were many troops of captives, and it would not have been enough for a single captivity to be restored unless all the dispersed were collected into one body. Before your eyes he takes as an assurance that they should witness a miracle they could hardly conceive without raising their thoughts above the world. Wesley carries the promise forward, that the universal church of the firstborn will be such in the great day, and the Israel of God be made a name and a praise to all eternity.
